doc.title: Johnny Varro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Pop music and radio in the 1950s
summary: Pop hits mixed with swing on radio; Fred Robbins and WNEW.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Wow. So you’re kind of now establishing yourself as a jazz piano player. And I’m curious what influence the current pop trends at the time—
At that time would have on what you guys needed to play on a job. Was there any?

I guess I’m meaning things like that would be on the AM radio at the time, either the beginnings of rock & roll, I guess I’m moving later into the 50s or “How Much is that Doggie in the Window” kind of things that were hits back then. Did they have any influence?

Probably not. They probably pushed me into the direction of real jazz. And get that away from me. Doggie in the Window. There was, well you know you’d turn the radio on and you’d hear Doggie in the Window and the next thing would be a Benny Goodman tune or a Tommy Dorsey big band thing or some small group. You’d hear, they mixed it up quite a bit. It wasn’t so personal now.
Yeah. So that was really part of the pop music, popular.

Yeah, Goodman and some of those things. You’d hear a trio and you’d listen to Make Believe Ballroom and some of those shows, William B. Williams especially in New York, WNEW had a lot of that stuff going on and later on Fred Robbins took over and was playing mostly jazz.
I see. So you didn’t really have to search the dial to find jazz oriented music like you do now?
Well you know, there wasn’t anything like a real jazz show where it was all jazz. You know I don’t think there was. There might have been — Fred Robbins might have been
one of the first to put a lot of jazz together, compile it in one section, in one half hour thing or an hour program.
